One of the simpler and accurate is dating Zircon crystals. During the crystals formation all lead is pushed out but some uranium is probably in the crystal at very low levels. Uranium decays into lead which is now trapped in the crystal. Two different isotopes of uranium decay into two different isotopes of lead giving two age lines that cross.

I'll try to rephrase what @drakesdoom said.

Lead does not dissolve in zircon. So when a zircon crystal is first formed, you can assume it will have no lead at all.

It will contain uranium. But uranium comes in two isotopes, each with a different decay rate and different decay products. So by measuring the amount of uranium and lead, you have two fairly independent measures of the age of the crystal, one for each U isotope.
So are you saying a certain isotope of Uranium can only become a certain isotope of Lead?

Lead-206, Lead-207, and Lead-208 only occur at the end of an Uranium isotope's decay chain, while Lead-204 occurs without radioactive decay. So by the relative amounts of Lead isotopes in a sample, an estimate on the sample's age can be made knowing the half-life of parents in the chain.

Very interesting! Can you explain how we can use spectroscopy to determine the composition of the universe?

Well, every atom and molecule in existence can be excited by light at a few very specific frequencies. Explanation here and click on any element to see its spectrum. This is only visible, but it extends in IR and UV. These lines are a "fingerprint" for every element in existence.

When we look at the universe, we can see that light gets absorbed (or emitted, depending on context) at these very specific frequencies. For example, we discovered helium by observing its spectral lines in sunlight (from where it got its name). By studying many different stars, nebulas, gas clouds, dust clouds or even entire galaxies, we can study what elements occur most where in the universe.

Combined with the knowledge of how nuclei are fused in stars and how stable different isotopes are, we can get a fairly accurate picture of what we can find where.
